I am a journeyman lineman in the northwest. What ya want to know?
How'd you get into that line of trade?

Going to a line school . These are programs that give you a basic understanding of line work. Tuition is anywhere from 6 to 10k. Once completed you would be certified to climb, drive truck ( CDL) and running derick trucks. Once you finish school, utilitys or PUD might have job offers starting as a ground man. Or you could go to a union hall sign the books as a ground man until you become an apprentice. An apprenticeship is usually 3 years of school and 7000 hours of practical work you get while on the job. A lot of utilities off pre apprenticeship programs where you work on the ground learning the trade until you become an apprentice. Depending on the route you want to take , it a good paying job with lots of rewards. This is just a rough overview on how it all works though. Hope it's a start.

I have a dawes lighting 1000 (Yup, a bikesdirect bicycle) with many thousand miles over four years. Thank god BikesDirect gave me the original manuals for the derailleurs. The job took a little over two hours, lots of flipping the bicycle over upside down too. Fun :)

A crank remover, a shimano bottom bracket tool, and a lock ring tool.

Doing your own repairs is satisfying. I recently ended up replacing almost the entire drivetrain on one of my bikes. I didn't do it all at once... everything just started going wrong right around the same roughly two week period, and I dealt with it at each step with a little advice from the guys at my LBS to guide me. That's what happens when you buy a cheap bike. Everything started to wear out after the first thousand miles. So that's the rear cassette, the crank arms and chain rings, the pedals, the bottom bracket, and of course the chain itself.

The only thing that feels better than a fresh smooth drivetrain is knowing that it got that way thanks to your own handiwork.
